a: We have been justified by faith
t: Justified: declared right, or made right?
p: Paul's courtroom word. This part meets it again in 5:9, 5:16-18, 6:7, 8:30 and 8:33.
b: The Greek verb dikaioo comes from the law court: to give a verdict in someone's favor. The fuller treatment of "justify," "righteousness" and "faith" is at 3:21-31 and 4:1-25 (an earlier part of this book); this note only follows the word through chapters 5-8. Here it names the starting point: those who trust Christ stand acquitted before God, and so they have peace (5:1), are saved from the coming anger (5:9), and cannot be accused (8:33). The churches have long disagreed about whether the verb means "declare right" (Lutheran and Reformed teaching) or "make right" by an inward change (Augustine and the Council of Trent), or both together. Paul himself uses the verb once in a way that fits neither easily: "The one who has died has been freed from sin" (6:7) is the same verb.

t: Peace: shalom and the Roman peace
p: A Hebrew word for wholeness, said in a city that boasted of the Roman Peace.
b: Paul's word eirene stands for the Hebrew shalom: not just no fighting but well-being, a relationship put right (Isaiah 57:19; Isaiah 52:7, which Paul quotes in Romans 10:15). Rome's own boast was the Pax Romana, a peace Augustus claimed to have won by victory and which the emperor's coins and altars advertised. Readers in the capital would feel the contrast: here is a peace that is not won by defeating enemies but by an enemy being reconciled (5:10). The two sides of the peace are in the next verses. Peace "with God" ends the war that Paul described in 1:18-3:20, and it opens the door to the peace of mind that comes in 8:6.

t: Access: being brought in to the king
p: The Greek word was used for being introduced to a ruler, or for bringing an offering near God.
b: Prosagoge, "access" or "introduction," is a court word: someone is brought in to a ruler. The related verb prosago is used in the Greek Old Testament for bringing offerings and priests near to God. Paul says that Christ is the one who brings us in (compare Ephesians 2:18; 3:12; 1 Peter 3:18). The next phrase gives the place where we now "stand": grace itself, as in a house or on solid ground. The perfect tense of "have been led in" and "stand" means the standing continues now. Paul will use "standing" and "falling" again at 11:20 and 14:4.

p: Paul has banned boasting in his own merits (3:27). Here he boasts in hope, in troubles and in God.
b: The Greek kauchaomai means both "boast" and "rejoice proudly in." In the earlier chapters boasting was the mark of the person who relied on being Jewish or on keeping the law (2:17, 23; 3:27; 4:2). Now Paul gives it a new object three times: the hope of God's glory (5:2), troubles (5:3), and God himself (5:11). He is following Jeremiah's line that the only proper boast is in knowing the LORD (Jeremiah 9:23-24). The verb is the same in all three places, so the English "boast" is kept, though "rejoice" would read more softly. The point is that the believer's pride has changed address.

t: The glory lost, the glory hoped for
p: Romans 3:23 said everyone falls short of God's glory. Here that lost glory becomes a hope.
b: At 3:23 (earlier part) Paul said that all "fall short of the glory of God." Jewish writers of Paul's time spoke of a glory that humans were meant to have and lost with Adam. The Community Rule from Qumran promises the faithful "all the glory of Adam" (1QS 4:23, reported in the standard translations), and the Damascus Document says the same (3:20). Psalm 8:5 says that humans are crowned "with glory and majesty." Paul uses the thought for the whole argument of chapters 5-8: the glory lost in Adam (5:12) is given back through Christ (8:17-21, 30). Here it is only a hope; by 8:30 it is spoken of as done.

p: Trouble, endurance, tested character, hope: a linked chain, and a Jewish-Christian habit of speech.
b: Paul builds a ladder: trouble (thlipsis, pressure) builds endurance (hypomone, "staying under the weight," active steadiness and not passive patience), endurance builds tested character, and tested character builds hope. Other writers use the same kind of chain: James 1:2-4 and 1 Peter 1:6-7 reach very similar conclusions, and the Wisdom of Solomon says that God tested the righteous like gold in a furnace (Wisdom of Solomon 3:5-6). Paul has his own troubles in mind (the beatings and hardships of 2 Corinthians 11:23-28), and he expects the Roman believers to meet theirs (8:35). The chain starts with something we would never choose and ends in hope; Paul does not say suffering is good, only that it can be used.

p: A word for metal that has been assayed and found genuine.
b: The Greek dokime comes from the test of a metal for purity. Proverbs puts the same picture in the LORD's hand: Silver is refined in the melting pot and gold in the furnace, "but it is the LORD who puts hearts to the test" (Proverbs 17:3). Paul uses the noun for the proved worth of a person or a church (2 Corinthians 2:9; 8:2; 9:13; Philippians 2:22). English versions say "character" or "proven character." The point of "tested" is that the goodness has been through fire and has come out unchanged.

a: poured God's love out into our hearts
t: God's love for us, or our love for God?
p: Whose love is it? Augustine and Aquinas said it is the love God gives us for him.
b: "The love of God" can mean God's love for us or the love for God that he puts in us. The surrounding verses (5:6-8, 8:35-39) are about God's love for us, and that is the reading most Protestant commentators take. Augustine took it as the love by which we love God, which the Spirit gives, and this reading (caritas poured into the heart) fed Catholic teaching on grace (compare Catechism 733). Both agree that the Spirit is the one who brings the love in. "Poured out" is the language of the Spirit's gift at Pentecost (Acts 2:17, 33; 10:45). This is also the first time in Romans 1-4 that the Holy Spirit is spoken of as a gift to every believer, and chapter 8 builds on it.

p: The Greek says 'according to the right moment', the same thought as Galatians 4:4.
b: Kairos is a fitting moment, not just a point on a clock. Galatians 4:4 speaks of the "fullness of time" (a letter to a different church), and Mark 1:15 of the time being fulfilled. For Paul the death of Christ comes at a time God picked. Christians have also noticed the timing in Roman history: the peace of Augustus and the Roman roads were already in place for the spread of the message, though Paul does not say so. The people Christ died for are called "weak and helpless" and "the ungodly." The last word is the same as in 4:5, where God "justifies the ungodly."

p: Paul separates a 'righteous' person from a 'good' one. Scholars disagree on how much.
b: The verse sets two kinds of people side by side: the "righteous" (dikaios), who does what is right and owes nothing, and the "good" one (ho agathos, with the article), who may be a benefactor. Cranfield and Moo treat this as two kinds of people, with the second kind more likely to move someone to die for him; others think the two words are near neighbors and the sentence is only a rhetorical step toward 5:8. Greek stories honor those who died for friends or country (Plato's Symposium praises Alcestis, who died for her husband), so Paul's readers knew that such a thing might happen, rarely. The point of 5:8 is that Christ's death was for people who were neither righteous nor good.

p: The verb means to put on display so that no one can doubt. The cross is the display.
b: Synistemi means to establish, recommend or demonstrate (the KJV has "commendeth"). The present tense is important: the cross is a standing proof, not only a past event. The order of the verse matters too. God does not wait for sinners to improve; the proof of his love is that Christ died while they were still sinners. The little word "for us" (hyper hemon) is where the churches' theories of the atonement divide: "on our behalf," "in our place," or both. The fuller discussion of what Christ's death does is at 3:25 (an earlier part). Here Paul only says that it shows love.

p: Blood stands for a life given up. The Old Testament sacrifices lie behind it.
b: In the Old Testament, blood is the life (Leviticus 17:11), and the blood of the Passover lamb marked those who would be spared (Exodus 12:13). When Paul says "his blood," he means the death of Christ seen as a sacrifice that covers sin; he has just used the same language at 3:25 (an earlier part). Paul's readers in Rome included Jews who knew these rituals and Gentiles who knew pagan blood sacrifices, and both would hear in "blood" a death that does something. The phrase "justified by his blood" sits next to "justified by faith" (5:1) without any strain: the blood is the ground, faith the way it is received.

t: The anger, and when it comes
p: The Greek says only 'the anger'. It is God's final reaction to sin, which Paul first mentioned in 1:18.
b: Paul writes simply "the anger" (he orge); English versions supply "of God," as the Plain does, because the same word in 1:18 and 2:5 is "God's anger." Most readers take it as the final judgment, "the day of anger" of 2:5 (compare 1 Thessalonians 1:10). C. H. Dodd read it as an impersonal moral process in which sin brings its own results; most commentators (Cranfield, Moo, Dunn) answer that Paul treats it as the personal response of a just God. Either way, the point here is that those who are justified need not fear it. See the topic on God's anger. "Saved" in this verse is in the future: Paul uses "saved" for what is still to come (also 13:11).

p: A word from relationships and diplomacy. Does God change, or we, or both?
b: Katallasso and katallage come from the world of broken friendships and warring parties, and the Greek Jewish books use them for God and his people: 2 Maccabees prays that God "be reconciled with you" (1:5) and says that after a short anger "he will make peace again with his own servants" (7:33). Paul says "enemies" (compare 11:28, where Israel is "enemies" because of the gospel and still loved). The question is whose hostility ends. Some (Leon Morris, Hodge) say God's anger is turned away; others say human hostility is overcome; Cranfield and Moo say both, since in Paul's picture hostility runs in both directions (1:18; 8:7).

p: His death reconciled us; his risen life keeps saving us.
b: The sentence is "how much more." If his death could do the harder thing, reconcile enemies, then his life can do the easier thing, save the reconciled. "His life" means the risen life of Christ, now at God's right hand and pleading for us (8:34). This is why the verse can say "will be saved" while 5:1 says we have been justified: both belong to one story, with the end still to come. "In" can also mean "by," so the translation could read "saved by his life."

a: sin entered the world through one man
t: Adam: a person, a figure, or both?
p: Paul speaks of Adam as a man, and as a pattern. The text itself gives no verdict on the garden story.
b: Paul reads Genesis 3 as a story with consequences for all people, and this is the center of the whole Western debate over original sin (see the card below and the topic page on the fall). Readers take Adam differently. Many church fathers and the later confessions took Adam as the first individual man. The Catholic Catechism says the story in Genesis uses figurative language but states "a primeval event" (390). Karl Barth thought Adam was a figure for every person ("each of us is his own Adam"); Jewish writers about a generation after Paul (about AD 100), who could not have been known to the Roman readers, put it the same way: "each of us has become our own Adam" (2 Baruch 54:19), and 4 Ezra mourns that the fall "was not yours alone, but ours also" (7:118). Others see in Adam the picture of Israel, or of humanity chosen from earlier creatures. This site gives no verdict. Paul's argument works if Adam is the head of a family of humans, whichever way the first chapters of Genesis are read.
r: Genesis 3:1-24; 1 Corinthians 15:21-22; 1 Corinthians 15:45-49; 2 Baruch 54:19; 4 Ezra 7:118; Sirach 25:24; Wisdom of Solomon 2:24

p: Paul speaks of sin as a character: it enters, rules, finds an opening, kills.
b: Paul uses the singular "sin" (hamartia), not the plural of many sins, and gives it actions: it "entered" (5:12), "ruled" (5:21), will not "lord it over" you (6:14), "found its opening" (7:8, 11), "lives in me" (7:17, 20). He does not say that sin is a person or a spirit being; most scholars say this is a way of speaking of the power that holds people in its grip, a power with a life of its own (compare the way he treats "death" in the same verse). For this reason the Plain keeps "sin" in lower case everywhere. The idea has links to Genesis 4:7, where sin "crouches at the door."

t: Because all sinned: four ways to read the Greek
p: The Latin 'in whom all sinned' shaped Augustine. The Greek means 'because' or 'on the ground of which'.
b: The Greek is eph' ho pantes hemarton. Augustine, reading the Latin Bible, which had in quo omnes peccaverunt ("in whom all sinned"), took it that all sinned in Adam and share his guilt (Merits and Forgiveness of Sins 1.11-15); Ambrosiaster had already read it that way. Erasmus and later Catholic scholars saw that the Greek does not say "in whom." Most modern commentators (Fitzmyer, Cranfield, Moo, Dunn) take eph' ho as "because" (some allow "with the result that") and read "all sinned" as: all people sinned, with Adam. How that works is still the question. Readings: (1) all sinned in Adam, representatively or in his loins (Augustine, the Reformed confessions); (2) death came to all, and so all sinned, being weakened by mortality (the Greek fathers such as Chrysostom; the Orthodox "ancestral sin"); (3) all sinned as Adam did, by their own acts (Pelagius; compare 2 Baruch 54:19, written about AD 100); (4) both death and sin spread together. The sentence also leaves a "just as" without its "so also" until 5:18.
orig: ἐφ' ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον (eph' ho pantes hemarton)

p: A bookkeeping word, found once in the New Testament apart from Philemon 18.
b: Ellogeo is a bookkeeper's verb: to enter a charge in the account (Paul uses it in Philemon 18, "charge that to me"). Paul says that between Adam and Moses there was sin but no entry in the books, because there was no written law to be broken. Yet people died. So death was not the result of breaking the Mosaic law (5:14). The statement sits uneasily beside 2:12-15, where Gentiles without the law are judged by what is written on their hearts; scholars suggest that "not counted" means "not counted as a transgression of a command," not "not counted at all." The point of the verse is to show that death in the period of 5:13-14 proves a wider cause than Moses.

a: those who had not sinned the way Adam did
t: Adam's sin and the sin of the generations after
p: Adam broke a spoken command. The people from Adam to Moses did not have one.
b: The Greek calls Adam's sin a parabasis, a stepping across a line. In Genesis 2:16-17 Adam was given a command not to eat, and the penalty was death. The people after Adam, up to Moses, had no such command, yet death ruled over them as it did over him. The Greek says death ruled over "those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam's transgression." A few witnesses drop the "not" (see the variant), and the Plain keeps it. So death cannot come only from the breaking of an explicit command. Some (Augustine and Calvin are often cited) take "those who did not sin" as infants and others who could not sin as Adam did, so that death came from Adam's sin and spread without their own act; others that the people between Adam and Moses were sinners by a different standard (1:20; 2:14-15). The phrase is a puzzle even for ancient readers, and the Latin fathers and Greek fathers took it differently.
orig: ἐπὶ τῷ ὁμοιώματι τῆς παραβάσεως Ἀδάμ (epi to homoiomati tes parabaseos Adam)

a: Adam is a figure of the one who was coming
t: Adam as a type of Christ
p: A 'type' is a stamp or pattern. The pattern fits by contrast as well as likeness.
b: The Greek typos is the mark left by a stamp, then a model or pattern. Paul calls Adam the pattern of the "coming one" (the Messiah), and the next verses draw the likeness and the difference: one act with huge effects for all. Early Christian writers called this method "typology." Here the likeness is that one person's act affects many; the difference is that the effect of grace is far greater (5:15-17). Paul uses the same thought in 1 Corinthians 15:21-22, 45-49, where Christ is the "last Adam." Some Jewish texts of the time looked for the faithful to receive "all the glory of Adam" in the age to come (Community Rule 4:23): a restored glory for the group, not a coming Adam-like figure. Paul's idea differs: Adam is the pattern, and Christ is the one who comes.

p: 'The many' does not mean 'some'. In Hebrew and Greek it means a large number that may be everyone.
b: In 5:15 and 5:19 Paul says "the many," and in 5:12 and 5:18 "all people." The two are not opposites. Hebrew rabbim ("the many") can mean the whole large group, set over against the one: the Servant in Isaiah will "put the many in the right" (Isaiah 53:11). Joachim Jeremias argued from this that "the many" is inclusive. This is why interpreters who believe in a limited atonement read "the many" as those Christ chooses, while universalists read it as everyone (see the card at 5:18). The grammar of the sentence alone does not settle it.

t: Kings in the age to come
p: Death ruled as a king. Those who receive grace will rule.
b: Paul uses the verb basileuo, "rule as king," five times in 5:14-21: death rules (5:14, 17), sin rules (5:21), grace rules (5:21), and believers will rule "in life" (5:17). The language is political, and a reader in the capital of the empire would catch it. The hope is also Jewish: the saints will receive the kingdom (Daniel 7:18, 27). In Revelation 22:5 the servants of God "will rule." "Rule in life" seems to mean sharing in the reign of Christ over death and sin. Whether this starts now (6:12-14) or waits for the age to come, Paul leaves open; "will rule" is future.

p: Does the second 'all' mean everyone, or everyone who receives grace?
b: The parallel is exact in Greek: "to all people" for condemnation, "to all people" for justification. Universalists (Origen and Gregory of Nyssa have been read this way; the Reformed theologian Karl Barth is often discussed here, though he denied teaching it as a doctrine) take both alls at face value. Most Christian traditions say the second "all" is qualified by 5:17: it is "those who receive" the gift. Calvin wrote that Paul makes grace common to all, because it is offered to all, not because it in fact reaches all. Others, including some Lutherans, speak of an "objective justification" of all that faith receives. The question is on the card below.

p: It can be Christ's obedience on the cross, or his whole life of obedience.
b: The phrase dikaioma ("one act of righteousness" or "one righteous act") is set against "one trespass." Most commentators take it as the cross; others include the whole of Christ's obedient life (which later Protestant theology called his "active obedience," counted to the believer). Paul puts the obedience in 5:19; Philippians 2:8 says Christ was "obedient to death," and Hebrews 5:8 that he "learned obedience." The result is "justification that gives life": the verdict of acquittal that leads to life, the reverse of the sentence in Genesis 2:17. The same Greek word, dikaioma, is rendered three ways in this part: "justification" (5:16, the ruling of acquittal that follows many trespasses), "act of righteousness" (5:18) and "what the law rightly requires" (8:4). It is not the word behind "the justification that gives life" in 5:18, which is dikaiosis.

p: The Greek verb means to place in a position. Churches differ on what position.
b: Kathistemi means to set someone in a position or to appoint (it is used for appointing elders in Titus 1:5). So "the many were made sinners" can mean they were put in the class of sinners, counted as guilty with Adam (the Reformed view of imputation), or made corrupt by what Adam did (the Catholic and Orthodox view of a fallen condition), or placed under the power of sin. The verb is used again of the many who "will be made righteous," and the same debate follows: counted righteous, or really made so. Paul's parallel keeps both halves in step, so a church's reading of the first half usually decides its reading of the second.

p: Isaiah's Servant 'will make the many righteous'. Paul uses nearly the same words.
b: Isaiah 53:11 says "my servant, the righteous one, will put the many in the right" (many versions render the Hebrew verb 'make righteous'). Paul's "the many will be made righteous" (5:19) uses the same two ideas, "the many" and "righteous," and many scholars hear Isaiah's Servant behind the verse. The point of contrast is Adam's disobedience at the tree; Christ's obedience is seen in Philippians 2:8 and in the Gethsemane prayer (Mark 14:36). Paul takes it as clear that Jesus was without sin (2 Corinthians 5:21), and here the obedient one is the one who makes others righteous.

t: The law came in on the side
p: The verb means to come in alongside, as an extra. Why was the law given?
b: Pareiserchomai is "to slip in beside" (Galatians 2:4 uses it for false brothers who slipped in). Paul says the law was not the main act but came in alongside. The purpose clause "so that the trespass would multiply" is startling, and Jewish readers might hear it as saying that God gave the law to make people worse. Paul answers this directly in 7:7-13 (law is holy, but sin uses it) and in Galatians 3:19. Interpreters explain "so that" as purpose (God meant the law to bring sin to light and bring it to its worst, so grace could answer it) or as result (the law in fact produced more sin). Luther called this the "theological use" of the law.

p: Sin ruled in death; grace rules through righteousness. The picture is of two kingdoms.
b: The kingdoms are set side by side. Sin ruled "in the realm of death," and now grace rules "through righteousness" and leads to "eternal life" (literally "life of the age," the life of the coming age). "Righteousness" here is the gift of acquittal (5:17), so grace rules through a verdict of "in the right" and not by ignoring sin. The chapter ends with the refrain that closes every section of chapters 5-8: "through Jesus Christ our Lord" (5:21; compare 5:1, 5:11, 6:23, 7:25, 8:39).

a: Should we stay in sin so that grace may multiply?
p: Paul's imaginary opponent says what some had already been slandering him with (3:8).
b: Paul often raises an objection and answers it, the style of a teacher's argument (scholars call it the "diatribe"; Stanley Stowers has studied it closely). The objector here is not a real person but a stand-in. The charge was real, though: at 3:8 Paul says he had been slandered as teaching "let us do evil that good may come." And 5:20 gave the objector his opening. Paul answers with three points in this chapter: believers have died to sin (6:2-11), sin must not rule (6:12-14), and one is always a slave to something (6:15-23). Answering the objection takes the rest of the chapter, and it belongs to Paul's description of how grace works.

p: A short, sharp answer, used ten times in Romans. It is the style of a Greek teacher's lecture.
b: The Greek me genoito (literally "may it not happen") is a strong refusal, used here and at 3:4, 3:6, 3:31, 6:15, 7:7, 7:13, 9:14, 11:1 and 11:11. The Greek philosopher Epictetus used it in his lectures to wave off a false inference, which is why scholars link it to the style of a classroom debate. The older English "God forbid" (KJV) is a free rendering; the Greek does not mention God. After it Paul gives a reason (here "We died to sin"), not just a protest, and so each use opens a short argument.

p: A picture of being released from a master, not of becoming unable to sin.
b: "Died to sin" is not a claim that sin no longer tempts. In Paul's language, death ends a relationship: a slave who dies is out of the owner's reach, a wife whose husband dies is free (7:1-3). Sin is here a master (5:21; 6:6, 14), and the believer's death in Christ has taken him out of its hands. The verb is a past event (a single death, in baptism: 6:3-4), while the demands of 6:11-13 are still to be lived out daily. Paul's logic is "you have died, so do not live as if you had not." The Jewish saying that a dead man is "free from the commandments" (see 6:7) shows the same idea.

p: Paul speaks of baptism as something all of his readers know, though he had not been to Rome.
b: Paul assumes that all believers in Rome were baptized, and he says "baptized into" Christ, which means brought into his ownership and his story (compare "baptized into Moses" in 1 Corinthians 10:2, and Galatians 3:27). Water washing was known: Jews immersed to become clean (the mikveh), John baptized for repentance (Mark 1:4), and whether Jews already immersed Gentile converts in Paul's day is debated. What is new is that baptism is described as joining the death and resurrection of Jesus. The churches' differences over what baptism does are on the card below; the baptism cards at Acts 2:38 and 16:15 ask other questions of the same topic.
r: 1 Corinthians 10:2; 1 Corinthians 12:13; Galatians 3:27; Colossians 2:12; Acts 2:38; Mark 1:4

p: Burial was part of the earliest creed (1 Corinthians 15:4). Baptism is a burial.
b: The earliest summary of the gospel says Christ "died for our sins," "was buried," and "has been raised on the third day" (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Paul sees the baptized person as going through the same three steps. Whether the picture needs immersion is debated: Baptists say yes, since going under the water pictures burial; Calvin said the word "baptize" means to immerse and that the ancient church immersed, but that the form is not essential (Institutes 4.15.19); Catholics and Orthodox have both poured and immersed. The best-known ancient Christian practice, the triple immersion of the Orthodox, uses the picture. Colossians 2:12 repeats the image.

a: walk in a life that is new
p: To 'walk' is to live. The Hebrew word for walking gave Jewish law its name.
b: "Walk" (peripateo) for a way of life is Hebrew, not Greek: the verb halak is used for living before God (Genesis 5:22; Psalm 1:1). The word for Jewish legal teaching, halakhah, comes from it: "the way one walks." So Paul is saying that the new life has its own halakhah: a way to walk. In 8:4 "walk by the Spirit" is the content. "The Father's glory" is God's powerful presence at work, as in the rescue at the Sea (Exodus 14:17-18); here it raises Christ.

t: Grown together, and the future tense
p: The word comes from plants: grafted or planted together. And 'will be' may be future or logical.
b: Symphytos means "grown together" or "planted together" and fits a vine or graft. Paul's picture is that the believer shares Christ's death like a plant joined to a stock. The second half, "we will certainly be part of his resurrection," is in the future tense. Is that the bodily resurrection at the end (many commentators say yes, since Paul keeps the new life of this age apart from the resurrection to come: 8:11, 23), or a logical future meaning "it follows that we also rise now to new life" (Dunn)? 6:4 already speaks of walking in new life, which may support the second reading; 6:8 ("we will also live with him") may support the first. Both may be true at once.

p: 'The old person' is the Adam in us: who we were under sin's rule.
b: Ho palaios anthropos is literally "our old person." After the Adam-Christ contrast in 5:12-21, this is the person who belongs to the old age ruled by Adam: sin and death. It is the same phrase in Ephesians 4:22 and Colossians 3:9. It is not "the old nature" (a modern idea of a part inside us) but the old way of being human, now "crucified with him." The new self is not named here, but 6:4 speaks of "newness of life." What remains is a struggle, not a division: 8:13 shows that the old life still pulls.
orig: ὁ παλαιὸς ἡμῶν ἄνθρωπος (ho palaios hemon anthropos)

t: 'Body of sin': the body ruled by sin
p: Not 'the sinful body', but the body as the place where sin rules. Paul speaks of sin as a power.
b: The Greek is to soma tes hamartias, literally "the body of sin" (KJV). It does not say that the body is sinful or bad; Paul expects bodies to be raised (8:11, 23). "Of sin" is read as "ruled by" or "belonging to" sin: the body as the place where sin has its power (compare 6:12, "your mortal body"). The verb that follows, katargeo, is "make powerless" or "put out of work"; it is the same word used of the law at 7:2, 6. As in 5:12 and 7:8-11, Paul writes about sin as a ruler with its own plans, and the Plain's wording keeps that in view. Paul is not teaching the Greek idea that the body is the problem; the problem is the power that rules it.
orig: τὸ σῶμα τῆς ἁμαρτίας (to soma tes hamartias)

a: The one who has died has been freed from sin
p: The verb is the one translated 'justify' elsewhere. A later rabbinic saying also says a dead man is free of the commandments.
b: The Greek is dedikaiotai, "has been justified," the verb of 5:1, 9. Here it means "acquitted, set free from a claim," and the Plain says "freed" with a gloss. Paul uses a well-known idea: death ends obligation. A later rabbinic saying, recorded in the Talmud (about AD 200-600, so after Paul), has "once a man has died he is free from the commandments" (Shabbat 30a; Niddah 61b). Paul is not quoting it; it shows that the same principle was current in Jewish thought. The rabbis meant that the dead no longer owe the commandments; Paul uses the principle for a death shared with Christ. The use also shows that "justify" in Paul is not limited to "declare righteous": it also means "set free from a charge."

a: Death no longer lords it over him
p: The verb comes from the word 'Lord'. Death was a master; Christ is now the Lord over it.
b: Kyrieuo is "to be lord over," from kyrios, "Lord." The same verb returns at 6:14, "sin will not lord it over you." Death had a claim on Christ in the sense that he truly died (5:6, 8), but by rising he left that rule behind. The line also echoes 5:14, 17, where death "ruled." This is among the clearest places where Paul treats the resurrection as a change of rulers: Christ is Lord, and death is not.

p: The Greek word appears in Hebrews for the sacrifice that never needs repeating.
b: Ephapax ("once for all") is used of Christ's death here and in Hebrews 7:27, 9:12 and 10:10. It means that his death can never be repeated or added to. The phrase "he died to sin" is hard: Christ was not a sinner, so what does it mean for him to die to sin? Most commentators say his death ended his time under sin's reign over mortal humanity (compare 8:3, "in the likeness of flesh that sin rules," and 2 Corinthians 5:21). Others say it means that he died for sin. The next phrase, "he lives to God," names the other side of the same event.

a: Think of yourselves in this way too
p: A bookkeeper's verb. 'Think of yourselves' means to take the accounts as they stand.
b: Logizesthe is the accounting verb that runs through chapter 4 ("credited as righteousness") and 8:18 ("I add it all up"). Here it is a command: take your accounts as they now stand. Paul has described what is true (6:2-10: you died with Christ). The command to "count" yourselves that way follows, and then the commands of 6:12-13. This pattern, "become what you are," is often called the indicative and the imperative: first what God has done, then what you are to do.

p: The Greek word means a soldier's weapons, and also tools in general.
b: Hopla can be "weapons" (a soldier's arms) or "tools"; the same word is used in 13:12 of "the weapons of light" and in 2 Corinthians 6:7. The picture is of a person who hands over the "parts" of the body (melē, hands, eyes, tongue: compare 3:13-16 and 7:5, 23) to a commander. The Plain says "weapons" because of the military language of 7:23 ("fights against," "takes me prisoner") and 13:12; "tools" is also possible, with the emphasis on service. The verb "hand over" is the same as in 6:16, 19, where it means to present oneself as a slave to a master.

a: You are not under law. You are under grace.
t: 'Under law': whose law, and who is under it?
p: Scholars differ on whether 'under law' means the Mosaic law-age, or the Gentile's position, or both.
b: "Under law" (hypo nomon) is a Pauline phrase (also in 3:19; 6:15; 1 Corinthians 9:20; Galatians 3:23; 4:4-5). Readings differ. (1) The traditional Protestant reading: believers are free from the law as a way to earn favor, but not from its moral guidance (Calvin's "third use"). (2) The New Perspective: "under law" is the period or condition of life under Mosaic rule, the era of Israel before Christ (Dunn, Wright). (3) "Paul within Judaism" readers (Nanos, Gager, Campbell and others) argue that Paul is writing to Gentiles, who were never under the Sinai covenant; Jewish believers are not told to leave Torah. The question is whom the law bound: the Torah bound Israel, not the nations (Deuteronomy 4:8; Romans 2:14). The notes on Romans in the Jewish Annotated New Testament give a Jewish scholar's view.

t: Slavery in Rome: the picture Paul's readers knew
p: Many believers in Rome were slaves or freed slaves. The picture would not have been abstract.
b: Many of the people in the Roman house churches were enslaved or had been (see the names in chapter 16, part of this book). A slave was handed over by sale, obeyed, and could be freed only by an act of the owner; freed slaves often kept ties of duty to the former owner. Paul uses this picture to say that no one is free of all masters: you are the slave of what you obey. This is not an endorsement of slavery. Paul uses a human picture and apologizes for its weakness (6:19). The Plain keeps "slave" because "servant" hides what the word meant; see the note at 1:1 (earlier part). For the later use of Romans in slavery debates, see the topic on slavery.

a: the form of teaching that you were handed over to
p: The wording is backward: the believers were handed over to the teaching, as if it were a master.
b: The Greek says you obeyed the "form of teaching" (typos didaches) "to which you were handed over." The expected sentence would be "the teaching that was handed over to you," as in 1 Corinthians 11:23 and 15:3 ("I handed on to you"). Paul has turned it around: the teaching is the master, and you were handed over to it, as slaves are. It is likely that "form of teaching" refers to the teaching given to new believers before baptism. Another reading takes the "form" as a mold into which the believer is poured.
orig: εἰς ὃν παρεδόθητε τύπον διδαχῆς (eis hon paredothete typon didaches)

a: I am speaking in human terms, because your flesh is weak
p: Paul admits that slavery is a poor picture, and the 'weakness' of flesh here is limited understanding.
b: Paul is aware that comparing life with God to slavery is an imperfect human picture (the Greek says "in a human way"). "Your flesh is weak" means that the readers' understanding is limited, not that they are sinful; compare "weak in the flesh" for the human condition. Paul also says: as you were slaves of lawlessness (which led to more lawlessness), so be slaves to righteousness (which leads to holiness). Holiness, hagiasmos, can mean the process of being set apart for God or the state of being set apart; Wesleyan and Reformed readers differ on which Paul means here. The two-sided picture is among the clearest signs that Paul does not make freedom the opposite of obedience.

a: things that now make you ashamed
p: In 1:16 Paul said he was not ashamed of the gospel. Here he says what believers are ashamed of.
b: The shame is a mark of the new life: the believers see their former way for what it was. It is the opposite of 1:16 ("I am not ashamed of the good news") and 5:5 ("hope does not make us ashamed"). The three kinds of fruit come in turn: what you had then (the fruit that ends in death), the fruit that leads to holiness (6:22), and the end, eternal life. "Fruit" is a harvest word and it is the Bible's usual picture of results (Psalm 1:3; Galatians 5:22).

p: The word for 'wages' was a soldier's pay. Sin pays what is earned; God gives what is not.
b: The Greek opsonia was the ration or pay given to a soldier (Luke 3:14; 1 Corinthians 9:7). Sin is a commander who pays his troops, and the pay is death. The contrast is the "gift" (charisma), grace freely given: the pay is earned, the gift is not. The Greek word for "gift" is related to "grace" (charis). The verse is well known for the line "the wages of sin is death," often read as a general law; in the context of chapter 6 it is more specific, the end of the service of a master. "Eternal life" is, in the language of the time, "the life of the age to come."

t: Which law, and who knows it?
p: Paul says 'law' without 'the'. Is it Moses' law, Roman law, or law in general?
b: The Greek has no article: "those who know law." Readings differ. It may mean law in general (a person is bound by law only while alive: true in Roman and Jewish law alike); or it may mean the law of Moses, known to the Jewish believers and to the Gentile "God-fearers" who had learned it in the synagogue. The Roman church had both groups. Since Paul has been writing about Moses' Torah all along, most commentators take the main sense as the Torah, with an example from marriage that everyone in Rome would know. The question of whom the Torah bound (Israel at Sinai, not the nations) matters here: see the setting cards.

p: A widow is free to marry. Jewish and Roman law agreed. Paul's application bends the picture.
b: In Jewish law a wife was bound to her husband until his death or a divorce document (the Mishnah, written down about AD 200 and so later than Paul, records the older rule: Kiddushin 1:1 says a woman "acquires herself" by a bill of divorce or by her husband's death). Roman law agreed that death ended a marriage. So the rule is an everyday one. The problem is the application in 7:4: in the illustration it is the husband who dies, but in the application it is the believers who "died" and the law that stays alive. Chrysostom saw this and observed that Paul chose not to say "the law died," to avoid giving offense to Jews. Others say Paul is not allegorizing, only borrowing the principle that death ends a bond. "Cleared of the law about the husband" is a legal phrase: released from the rule that bound her.

a: put to death in relation to the law
t: You were put to death to the law
p: A passive verb: someone else did it, and it was done 'through the body of Christ'.
b: The Greek is the passive ethanatothete, "you were put to death," and the dative "to the law" is a relationship: dead as far as the law is concerned. "Through the body of Christ" means through his death on the cross (not the church; the church as "body" is first named in 12:4-5). Galatians 2:19 says, "For I myself, through the law, died to the law." The verse does not say the law died or is bad; it says the believers' relation to it changed so they could belong to another, the risen Christ, and bear fruit for God. Many see a marriage image, with Christ as the new husband (compare 2 Corinthians 11:2; Ephesians 5:25-32).

t: Flesh: the human being on the side of sin
p: Paul uses 'flesh' for more than the body. It is life lived in the old age, apart from the Spirit.
b: Sarx, "flesh," has several senses in Paul. It is the physical body (2 Corinthians 12:7), the human being as weak and mortal (6:19), and, as here, human life in the old age, under the power of sin and cut off from the Spirit. The contrast "in the flesh" and "in the Spirit" (8:9) marks two ages, not two parts of a person. The term decision for this book is that the Plain never says "sinful nature" for sarx (an interpretation that hides the Greek). The word returns often: 7:14, 18, 25; 8:3-13. Modern scholars disagree on whether "flesh" always carries a moral meaning: Dunn thinks it shows a human condition of weakness that sin uses; Moo, a power-sphere.

p: The Greek can say 'we died to what held us', or 'what held us died'.
b: The standard Greek text (and the Plain) says "having died to that by which we were held," meaning we died. A rarer reading puts the participle in the genitive, "that by which we were held having died," which would say that the law died; the KJV's "that being dead wherein we were held" follows it. The Latin Vulgate has a third wording, "from the law of death in which we were held." All three are in the variant entry. The text says our relationship to the law ended because of our death with Christ, not that the law was abolished. Jewish believers could read this without hearing a rejection of Torah, since the point of 7:1-4 is that a death ends a bond. A later rabbinic teaching held that the commandments will be set aside in the age to come (Niddah 61b, about AD 500-600); Jeremiah 31:31-34 promises a new covenant but does not say that.

a: the old way of the written letter
p: Jeremiah's new covenant: the law written on hearts, and Ezekiel's new spirit. 'Letter' is not 'Torah is bad'.
b: "The written letter" (gramma) against "the Spirit" (pneuma) has two backgrounds. Jeremiah 31:33 promises "I will put my law inside them, and on their hearts I will write it"; Ezekiel 36:26-27 promises a new spirit. Paul takes up the same contrast in 2 Corinthians 3:6. Augustine's On the Spirit and the Letter read "the letter" as the law without the help of grace, "that kills" because it commands what it cannot give. Origen read "letter" as the surface meaning of Scripture and "spirit" as its deeper sense. Jewish readers of the passage often stress that Paul does not condemn the Torah but contrasts two ways of serving it; Pamela Eisenbaum and Mark Nanos stress this, while others (Dunn, Moo) think Paul does see the old covenant as ended in some way.

p: A second defense of the law. The first was 3:31.
b: This is the question the end of chapter 5 invited ("the law slipped in so that the trespass would multiply") and chapter 6 prepared (6:14: "not under law"). Paul's answer is "By no means!" and then a narrative: the law shows sin for what it is. A parallel Jewish idea, found later than Paul in the Talmud (about AD 500-600), says the law is an antidote to the evil inclination (God says, "I created the evil inclination; I created the Torah as its antidote," Kiddushin 30b). Paul agrees that the law is good, but says sin uses it. The book of Romans keeps returning to this defense of the Torah (3:31; 7:12, 14; 8:4; 9:4; 13:8-10).

p: Why Paul picks this commandment: it is about desire, not an act.
b: Paul quotes the last of the Ten Words, which this site translates "You must not crave your neighbor's house" (Exodus 20:17; Deuteronomy 5:21). The Greek version has ouk epithymeseis, "You shall not desire." Why this commandment? It is the only one that forbids an inner desire, not an outward act, so it shows that sin is in the heart. Jewish writers of Paul's time noticed this: 4 Maccabees uses the command as an example of the mastery of reason over desire (2:5-6), and Philo called desire the source of all sins (On the Decalogue 142-153, 173). Paul gives no object ("your neighbor's house"); the word stands alone, which makes the command general.

a: Sin found its opening in the commandment
t: An opening, a base of operations
p: Sin is pictured as an army that takes a position (as in 5:12, 6:6).
b: Aphorme is "a starting point" and, in military language, a base of operations. Sin is written as an invader that uses the commandment as its base: the command "do not" makes the forbidden thing attractive and gives sin something to work with. As in 5:12 and 6:6, Paul speaks of sin as a character with plans. The line "without law, sin is dead" means inactive, not nonexistent (compare 5:13: sin was in the world before the law). Ovid wrote that we strive for what is forbidden (Amores 3.4.17); Paul makes the same pull a statement about the law's relation to sin.

p: The first-person story points to Adam, Israel at Sinai, Paul as a child, or every person.
b: When was the "I" alive without law, and when did the commandment "come"? Readings: (1) Adam, who lived before the command and died when he broke it (Genesis 2:17), since 7:11 echoes Eve's words "The snake fooled me" (Genesis 3:13); (2) Israel before and at Sinai; (3) Paul as a child, before he reached the age of responsibility (the Mishnah says "at thirteen for the commandments," Avot 5:21, though that is a later teaching); (4) a literary "I," a character any reader can enter (Kümmel, 1929; Stowers argues for "speech in character"). Many hold that more than one is true. See the deep dive on this page. In Jewish writing the first-person "I" is common in psalms and in confession, and does not need to be the author's autobiography.

p: A close relative of the verb Genesis uses of Eve and the snake.
b: The verb exapatao is the same root, with a prefix, as the verb the Greek Old Testament uses of the snake's deceit: "The woman answered, 'The snake fooled me, and I ate'" (Genesis 3:13, where the Greek has apatao). The "I died" at 7:9-11 echoes God's warning, "on the day you eat from it you will die" (Genesis 2:17). Paul used the same verb for Eve in 2 Corinthians 11:3. These echoes are the strongest evidence for those who find Adam in the "I" of 7:7-13. Sin is the snake, the commandment the tree, and the result is the same, death. Whether Paul only borrows the story or means Adam himself, he has written the chapter with Genesis open.

t: The law is holy, righteous and good
p: A strong defense. Paul's words about the law have to be read with this verse in mind.
b: Three adjectives, holy, righteous, good, close the defense. "Holy" echoes Leviticus 19:2 and the Torah's claim; "good" is what Deuteronomy 30:15 says of the law's way. In Paul's own letters the sharp statements about the law (5:20; 7:5) sit beside defenses like this one (3:31; 7:14; 8:4). Marcion (second century), who thought the God of the law was a lesser god, built his case on Paul's sharp sayings about the law (Tertullian, Against Marcion); this verse and 3:31 are what such a reading has to explain away. Scholars who read Paul within Judaism (Fredriksen, Eisenbaum, Nanos) point to this verse as proof that Paul never rejected the Torah for Jews. Whether he held it binding on Gentiles is a different question, taken up in Galatians and 1 Corinthians 7:19. "Law" and "commandment" are here two words for the same thing.

p: From 7:14 the verbs turn to the present. And the Greek for 'flesh' is a different form.
b: Up to 7:13 the verbs were past ("I died"). From 7:14 they are present ("I do"). Does this mean Paul now describes a continuing struggle in a Christian (Augustine's later view, Luther, Calvin, Cranfield, Murray, and Dunn in his own way) or is a "historical present" for a vivid story of life before Christ (Kümmel and the Greek fathers)? The tense settles little by itself. The word "made of flesh" (sarkinos) differs from "fleshly" (sarkikos) by its ending: "-inos" is "made of," "-ikos" is "characterized by"; the Byzantine text has the second (see the variant). The cards below give the reading of each church tradition.

a: I do not recognize what I do
p: The Greek verb for 'know' can also mean to acknowledge or approve.
b: The verb is ginosko, "know." The Plain says "recognize" to keep both senses open. In Greek and Hebrew speech, "to know" can mean "to acknowledge, to approve": Psalm 1:6 says the Lord "knows" the way of the righteous, and Jesus says "I never knew you" (Matthew 7:23). Many commentators hear that sense here: "I do not approve what I do." Others hear the plain sense, "I do not understand myself." Either fits the next line, "What I want to do, I do not do."

p: 'Sold' is Israel's language for the people of the exile and the wicked king.
b: The verb pipraskomai, "sold," is the Old Testament language for people who give themselves over to evil: Elijah tells Ahab, "because you sold yourself to do what the LORD sees as evil" (1 Kings 21:20; compare 2 Kings 17:17). Isaiah 50:1 says Israel was "sold" for its sins. For Paul's readers the picture is of the slave market (6:16-19): the "I" is a slave who was sold. Paul does not say who sold him. This is the sharpest point of the contrast with 8:2, where "you" are set free.
orig: πεπραμένος ὑπὸ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν (pepramenos hypo ten hamartian)

a: What I want to do, I do not do
t: The divided will in Greek and Roman writing
p: Others in Paul's world described the same experience. They gave it a different cause.
b: The experience of knowing the better and doing the worse was well known. In Euripides' Medea (1078-80) Medea says she knows the evil she means to do, but her passion is stronger than her thought; Ovid has "I see the better and approve it; I follow the worse" (Metamorphoses 7.19-21); the Stoic Epictetus says of the person who does wrong, "what he wants, he does not do, and what he does not want, he does" (Discourses 2.26). These show that Paul's readers would recognize the experience. The difference lies in the diagnosis: for the Greek writers the cause is passion overcoming reason; for Paul it is sin as a power, using even the good law. Verdict: a real parallel in the experience, but no borrowing of Paul's explanation.

a: but the doing of it is not
p: The oldest Greek ends the sentence without a verb. Later copies added 'I do not find'.
b: The sentence in the earliest manuscripts ends bluntly: "the wishing is with me, but the doing of the good, no." The Byzantine text adds a verb ("I do not find how"), which is the KJV's "how to perform that which is good I find not." The Plain follows the shorter text. "That is, in my flesh" is a qualification that later readers made much of: Augustine, in his later view, used it to say that Paul speaks as a believer, whose "flesh" is only a part of him, not the whole. Others (Cranfield) say it limits "me" to the flesh as the area of failure.

p: Paul speaks of 'the law of God', 'the law of my mind', 'the law of sin', and here 'this law'.
b: The Greek nomos appears 28 times in chapters 7-8 (23 in chapter 7, 5 in chapter 8). Readings of "law" in 7:21, 23 and 8:2: (1) the Torah, seen from different sides; (2) a "rule" or "principle," the way English says "the law of gravity" (a choice many modern translations make: "principle"); (3) a mix (Dunn: the same Torah that sin turns to its own use). The Plain keeps "law" so the reader can see the repeated word and the possible play on it. At 7:21 the sentence is awkward: "I find this law: that, when I want to do good, evil is present with me." It can also mean "I find the principle that ...". Paul may be echoing the Jewish view that sin could not be separated from the Torah.

p: A Greek idea (Plato) that Paul uses. It is not the whole person.
b: "The inner person" (ho eso anthropos) is found in Plato (Republic 589a) and is taken up in Paul in 2 Corinthians 4:16 ("our inner person is made new, day after day") and Ephesians 3:16. Paul sets it against "the outer person" or the body. Here it is the part of "me" that agrees with God's law: the "mind" of 7:23, 25. Whether this belongs only to a believer is argued: Augustine in his later work and Calvin said it is the regenerate part of the Christian; Origen and Chrysostom said it is the person before grace, who can still agree with the good in his mind, as the Gentile of 2:14-15 does. The phrase echoes the psalmists' delight in the law of the LORD (Psalm 1:2; Psalm 119:77).

p: 'Another law', 'the law of my mind', 'the law of sin': Torah, or a rule at work?
b: Verse 23 names three laws: "another law" in the body's parts, "the law of my mind," and "the law of sin." Paul has just called the Torah "the law of God" (7:22, 25). Readings: (1) all use nomos as "principle" or "rule," a pattern that governs (the older translations "I find a law" in 7:21 are often explained so); (2) the mind's law is the Torah as the mind knows it, and "the law of sin" is the Torah as sin uses it, one Torah seen from two sides (Dunn, Wright); (3) a mix, with Paul playing on the word. See the notes at 7:21 and 8:2. The Plain keeps "law" so the reader sees the repeated word.

a: Who will rescue me out of this body of death?
t: The cry of the divided self
p: The cry ends the chapter's puzzle; the answer in 7:25 is a person.
b: The cry has two parts: "I am a wretched man" (talaiporos, a word of misery) and the question, "Who will rescue me?" The expression "this body of death" can mean the body doomed to die (7:5, 8:10), the self under the rule of death, or the body as the instrument of sin (6:6, "the body ruled by sin"). The answer comes in the next line, not "what" but "who": "through Jesus Christ our Lord." The cry is the climax of the self-portrait; in 8:1 the answer is stated as a fact. Whether Paul speaks for himself as a Christian, for the Jew under the law, or for Adam's children, the reply is the same.

a: So this is how it stands
t: Verse 25b: a conclusion, or a later addition?
p: The last line seems to undo the thanksgiving just before it. Some editors move or remove it.
b: After the thanksgiving of 7:25a the verse goes back to the divided condition: "with my mind I myself serve the law of God, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin." Readings: (1) it is Paul's summary of the whole picture of 7:14-24 before he turns to chapter 8; (2) it sums up the believer's continuing state (those who see the "I" as a Christian); (3) it is out of place, and some scholars move it before 7:24 or treat it as a note added later (Rudolf Bultmann argued this in 1947, as reported by commentators). No manuscript omits it. The Plain keeps it where it stands.

p: The verdict of 5:16 and 5:18 is reversed. 'Now' marks the change of age.
b: Katakrima is the sentence that follows a guilty verdict. In 5:16 and 5:18 it came to all through Adam's trespass. Here it is lifted from those "in Christ Jesus." The little word "now" (nyn) is the turn of the ages, as in 3:21 ("But now") and 5:9, 11. The verse also answers the cry of 7:24: the one who asked who would rescue him hears that no sentence stands. Verse 34 will ask who can "condemn," and the two verses frame the chapter. The Byzantine text adds a clause about walking by the Spirit; see the variant.

a: the law of the Spirit of life
p: Is 'the law of the Spirit' the Torah as the Spirit gives it, or a rule or power?
b: Paul speaks of "the law of the Spirit of life" and "the law of sin and of death." Readings: (1) "law" is a rule or power (Luther, Calvin, Cranfield, Moo in part): the working of the Spirit against the working of sin; (2) "law" is the Torah in both phrases, once as sin uses it (7:7-13) and once as the Spirit fulfills it (8:4, Dunn, Wright, Hays); (3) the law of faith (3:27) as a new Torah. The context in 8:3-4 speaks of the "righteous requirement of the law" fulfilled in us, which fits the second. The promise behind it is Jeremiah 31:33 ("I will put my law inside them") with Ezekiel 36:26-27. The word "you" is singular; some copies read "me" (see the variant).
orig: ὁ νόμος τοῦ πνεύματος τῆς ζωῆς (ho nomos tou pneumatos tes zoes)

a: because the flesh made it weak
p: The weakness is in the flesh, not in the law.
b: The law "was powerless" not because it was faulty but because "the flesh made it weak": it could tell people what to do but could not give them the power to do it. This matches 7:12 and 7:14: the law is "holy" and "spiritual," the "I" is "made of flesh." Paul sees a helpless situation that only God could change, and God "did what it could not." The same thought comes at Galatians 3:21 (if a law had been given that could give life, righteousness would have come from the law). So the verse corrects the idea that Paul blames the law.

a: in the likeness of flesh that sin rules
t: Likeness: was his flesh like ours?
p: Paul says 'in the likeness of flesh of sin'. The careful wording has been argued for 1,800 years.
b: The Greek is en homoiomati sarkos hamartias, "in the likeness of flesh of sin." Paul does not say "in sinful flesh" (that would suggest Christ sinned) and does not say "in the likeness of flesh" alone (that would suggest he only seemed human). He says Christ came in flesh like ours, the flesh that sin rules. That is how the Plain reads the genitive "of sin"; the literal "flesh of sin" leaves the relation open, and the dispute below turns partly on it. Disputes: Did he take on a nature already fallen (Edward Irving, Karl Barth, T. F. Torrance: he took our fallen nature, in order to heal it) or an unfallen human nature (the older Catholic and Reformed teaching)? The Eastern principle, stated by Gregory of Nazianzus, was "what is not assumed is not healed." Early Christians also used the line against docetism, the idea that Christ only seemed to have a body. Philippians 2:7 and Hebrews 2:14, 4:15 are the other main texts.
orig: ἐν ὁμοιώματι σαρκὸς ἁμαρτίας (en homoiomati sarkos hamartias)

p: The Greek phrase 'about sin' is the Septuagint's regular word for the sin offering.
b: The words peri hamartias ("concerning sin") are very common in the Greek Old Testament for the sin offering (hatta't, for example Leviticus 4:3 and 16:5). Hebrews 10:6, 8 uses the same phrase for the offering. So many commentators (Dunn, Wright, Moo, Cranfield) read "as a sin offering." Others read the phrase simply as "for sin" or "to deal with sin" (as some versions render it, with the sin-offering idea in a footnote); the Plain follows the first. The sin offering in Leviticus cleansed the sanctuary and the people from the effects of sin; for the Day of Atonement see Leviticus 16. The verb that follows, "condemned sin in the flesh," says that sin was judged in Christ's flesh, not that Christ was condemned.

a: what the law rightly requires would be fulfilled in us
p: Who fulfills it: Christians by the Spirit, or Christ for us? The churches differ.
b: The Greek dikaioma (the word of 5:16 and 5:18; see the note at 5:18) is singular, "the requirement" or "right ruling" of the law. Readings: (1) believers fulfill it in their lives by the Spirit, which is love (13:8-10), as the Reformed and most Catholic teachers say (Calvin's "third use"); (2) Christ's obedience is credited to believers as their fulfillment (Luther and others stress that "in us" does not mean "by us"); (3) in the new covenant the Torah's goal is realized in Spirit-led people, including Gentiles (Wright, Dunn). The phrase "walk not by the flesh but by the Spirit" in this verse is not a condition added to grace; it describes how the fulfillment looks. The passage is paired with the new-covenant promises of Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 36:27.

a: It does not submit to God's law
p: Paul uses 'submit' for the flesh and the law, and later for the governing authorities (13:1).
b: The verb hypotasso means to put oneself under an order, a rank. It is used again for creation (8:20), for Israel's refusal to submit to God's righteousness (10:3), and for submission to authorities (13:1, 5). It is kept distinct from "obey" (hypakouo; 6:16-17; 10:16; 16:19). Paul's point is that the mind set on the flesh is not neutral toward God's law: it cannot submit to it, as 7:14-25 has shown. The sentence presupposes that the Torah is "God's law" (compare 7:22) even in this sharp passage.

t: The Spirit of God, the Spirit of Christ, Christ in you
p: Three phrases for one reality. The early church built its teaching on the Spirit and the Trinity from verses like this.
b: In 8:9-11 Paul moves between "the Spirit of God," "the Spirit of Christ" and "Christ in you" without a break; 8:11 adds the Father as the one who raised Jesus. He assumes that all three belong together. Later theology took the verses as part of its foundation: the Spirit is not an impersonal force but belongs to God and to Christ. The Western church's addition of "and the Son" (filioque) to the creed's statement that the Spirit proceeds from the Father was defended by texts like this one; the Orthodox answer that the sending of the Spirit in time does not show the eternal relations. Galatians 4:6 has "the Spirit of his Son"; John 14:17-18 speaks of the Spirit and Jesus coming together.

a: the body is dead because of sin
p: Does 'the Spirit is life' mean God's Spirit or the human spirit?
b: The body is "dead because of sin" in the sense that it is mortal and under the sentence of death (5:12), though Christ is in the believer. "The Spirit is life": the capital letter is the translators' choice. Some read "spirit" (the human spirit) as alive because of righteousness, a parallel to the body; most read the Holy Spirit as the source of life. Either way the next verse gives the hope: the same Spirit will give life to the dead body. "Because of righteousness" means either the believer's justification or the right standing from God's verdict (5:17-18).

a: bring your mortal bodies to life
t: The Spirit who raises the dead
p: Ezekiel's valley of dry bones is the background: the Spirit enters and the dead live.
b: In Ezekiel 37 the LORD puts breath and spirit into dry bones and they live; the promise is that the LORD will put his spirit in them and they will live (Ezekiel 37:14). Paul says the Spirit who lives in believers will do the same to their "mortal bodies." This shows that Paul's hope is a bodily one, not a release of the soul from the body (compare 8:23, "the redemption of our bodies"). The raising of Jesus is the start and the model (1 Corinthians 15:20-23). The same Greek verb "to give life" is used for God who "gives life to the dead" in 4:17.

p: The Greek says 'sons' here and 'children' in 8:16-17. Both are used for all believers.
b: In 8:14 and 8:19 the Greek has huioi, "sons"; in 8:16, 17, 21 it has tekna, "children." The Plain says "children" for both so that the reader is not led to think women are left out. The word "sons" is used for all believers because a son was the heir in Roman and Jewish households: women and men, Jews and Gentiles, all share the status of heirs (Galatians 3:26-29; 4:5-7). Compare Israel as God's "son" (Exodus 4:22: "Israel is my son, my firstborn") and "You are children of the LORD your God" (Deuteronomy 14:1). The adoption language that follows (8:15) explains how Gentiles became such children.

a: the Spirit of adoption as children
p: Roman readers knew adoption as a public, legal act that gave a new name, a new family and a new inheritance.
b: Paul's word huiothesia ("placing as a son") is a term from Greek and Roman law; it does not appear in the Old Testament or the Jewish writings of the time. In Rome adoption was common, above all among the rich who needed an heir: the emperor Claudius adopted Nero in AD 50 (Tacitus, Annals 12.25-26), and Augustus himself was adopted by Julius Caesar. An adopted person gained the full rights of a son (Gaius, Institutes 1.97-107): a new family, a new name and a claim on the inheritance. Paul adds what Rome would not know: God adopts slaves (6:16-22; 8:15) and makes them heirs. Israel too had the right: "adoption" belongs to the Israelites (9:4). Scholars debate whether Paul's picture is Roman, Greek, or Israelite (James Scott argues for the Old Testament line of 2 Samuel 7:14).

p: Abba is Aramaic for 'father'. It is warm, but a popular claim that it means 'Daddy' has been given up.
b: Abba is the Aramaic word for father. Jesus prayed with it in Gethsemane ("Abba, Father," Mark 14:36), and Paul gives it here and in Galatians 4:6 as the cry of the Spirit. The German scholar Joachim Jeremias argued in the 1960s that it was a child's word, like "Daddy," and that Jesus' use of it was new. James Barr (1988) and others showed that this is not right: Aramaic abba was used by adult children as well, and no evidence supports "Daddy." It still means personal, direct address. Jews also called God "our Father in heaven" (Mishnah Sotah 9:15). Paul gives the Aramaic and the Greek (ho pater), a double form that may come from the bilingual prayer of the early churches.

p: Does the Spirit give a believer inner certainty of being God's child? Churches answer differently.
b: The Greek symmartyrei has two possible senses: the Spirit testifies "together with" our spirit, or "to" our spirit. In both, a testimony is given, and the traditions disagree about what it gives and how certain it is. John Wesley made "the witness of the Spirit" a main doctrine; the Reformed hold that a believer may have assurance by faith and the Spirit's seal; Catholic teaching (Trent) says no one can know with the certainty of faith that he has received grace unless God reveals it. The card at this verse gives the views side by side. The Roman court context adds something: a case before a magistrate needed two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15).

t: Heirs: inheritance in a Roman house
p: The adopted child inherits. The inheritance is God himself and the world to come.
b: In Roman law the heir took the estate; "joint heirs" (synkleronomoi) shared it. The inheritance for Israel was the land (Deuteronomy 4:21); Paul said Abraham would inherit "the world" (4:13, an earlier part). Here the heirs inherit "of God." The "if" is not a doubt but "since indeed" or "provided that": suffering with Christ is the road, not a bargain. The next line adds that glory comes after. For the Eastern church this verse, with 8:29-30, is the root of theosis, sharing in God's life; the Catholic Catechism quotes Athanasius's line that the Son of God became man "that we might become God" (460).

p: The accounting verb returns. The result of the sum: the sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory.
b: Logizomai is the accounting word used for crediting righteousness in chapter 4 and for "count yourselves" in 6:11. Here it is the opposite of a gloomy attitude: Paul calculates, and the total favors the future. He does not call the sufferings small; he says they do not weigh enough to be compared. In Jewish apocalyptic thought, the present age's pain and the age to come's glory are set against each other (4 Ezra 7:12-14; 2 Baruch 15:8; both written about AD 100, a generation after Paul, but in the same stream of thought). Paul's own record of sufferings (2 Corinthians 11:23-28) shows he is not speaking lightly.

p: Does it mean the non-human world, all creatures, or something else? The reading changes the passage.
b: Ktisis, "creation," is the subject for 8:19-22. Readings: (1) the non-human creation, the natural world (most modern commentators; Chrysostom among the Greek fathers; Calvin took it of the lower creatures); (2) all human beings (some ancient readers); (3) unbelieving humans; (4) angels, or the powers of the world (Origen's view that the creation includes heavenly beings). The words "not willingly" and "stands on tiptoe" (apokaradokia, "the stretched neck of one looking for something to appear") make most take it as the natural world. Isaiah 11:6-9 and 65:17-25 describe the hope for the animals and land. The details of 8:20, 21 and 22 fit the first reading best.

p: The Greek word for 'futility' is the Septuagint's word for Ecclesiastes' 'vapor'. And who subjected the creation?
b: Mataiotes, "futility," is the Septuagint's regular rendering of Hebrew hevel: in Ecclesiastes 1:2 this site renders hevel as "vapor," and Qohelet says that everything is vapor. Paul's picture is of a world that does not reach its goal. Who "subjected" it? Readings: God, in response to Adam's sin (Genesis 3:17-19: "the ground is cursed on your account"), which most take as the sense, since "not willingly" rules out the creation itself and "in hope" shows God's purpose; Adam himself; or Satan or the angelic powers (some ancient Jewish writings). The word "in hope" ends the sentence, linking to 8:21.

a: that the creation itself will also be set free
p: The little word can start the content of the hope or give a reason for it.
b: The Greek hoti after "in hope" can mean "that" (the hope is that the creation will be freed) or "because" (it was subjected in hope, because it will be freed). The first is more common. Either way, the freeing of the creation is joined to the glorification of God's children: the creation's liberation is linked to theirs, as its subjection was linked to Adam's. "Slavery to decay" (douleia tes phthoras) echoes the language of slavery in chapters 6-7. Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22 speak of new heavens and a new earth; 2 Peter 3:13 and Revelation 21:1 repeat the hope. Jewish and Christian writings of the time also speak of the restoring of creation.

a: all of creation groans as one and is in labor as one
t: Birth pangs, and the earth today
p: Labor pains are the picture of the old age giving birth to the new. Christians have read it for the environment.
b: The pains of childbirth were the Bible's picture for the pain that comes before God's new work (Isaiah 66:7-9; Mark 13:8). Later Jewish writing speaks of "the birth pangs of the Messiah." Paul says the whole creation shares the labor. Modern ecological readings use the verse to say that Christians should care for the creation, which suffers with humans: Greening Paul (Horrell, Hunt, Southgate) is one study, and Pope Francis opens his letter Laudato Si' (2015) with a reference to it. Others warn that Paul's focus is the hope of a transformed world, not the present management of nature. Both can be true.

p: The first part of the harvest, offered to God as a promise of the rest. Present adoption, future adoption.
b: The firstfruits were the first ripe produce, offered at the Feast of Weeks (Pentecost; Leviticus 23:15-21) as a pledge of the harvest to come. For Paul the Spirit is the firstfruits: the beginning that guarantees the rest (compare "down payment," 2 Corinthians 1:22). The Greek is "the firstfruits of the Spirit." The Plain reads it as "the Spirit as the firstfruits"; another reading takes it as a share: "the first share that the Spirit gives." The verse also holds a puzzle: adoption is already given (8:15) and still awaited (8:23), the redemption of the body. This "already and not yet" runs through Paul; the church lives between the two. The first fruits of the resurrection is Christ himself (1 Corinthians 15:20), and the Jewish festival gave the image to the church's Pentecost (Acts 2).

p: The word means being set free by a price paid. The body is what is redeemed, not escaped.
b: Apolytrosis, "redemption," began as the buying back of a slave or captive (Exodus 21:8 for a slave girl; Leviticus 25:25-55 for the family redeemer). Paul used it at 3:24 of the freedom Christ gave; here it names the final act: the body itself, mortal and groaning, is set free. This agrees with 8:11 and with the teaching about the resurrection in Philippians 3:21 and 1 Corinthians 15:42-54. The hope is not to leave the body behind, but to receive it back changed.

p: Paul says 'we were saved' here, 'we will be saved' in 5:9-10 and 13:11. All three belong together.
b: Paul uses "save" in three tenses: past (here, and Ephesians 2:5, 8), present ("being saved," 1 Corinthians 1:18) and future (5:9-10; 13:11). They are not in conflict. Salvation began when Christ's work was received, is going on, and will be complete at the end. "In hope" (or "by hope") means that our salvation is not all in hand: it is partly a promise. A hope that has been fulfilled is no longer hope (8:24b). The verse rules out any claim that the Christian life is already complete, which suited a church in the middle of a hard city.

t: The Spirit's groans: tongues, or something else?
p: Are these groans speaking in tongues? Most commentators say no; some Pentecostals and Käsemann say yes.
b: The Greek stenagmois alaletois can mean "unspeakable" (too deep for words) or "not spoken" (wordless). Käsemann argued that the groans are the Spirit's own speech, expressed in ecstatic language, i.e., tongues. Pentecostal and charismatic teachers often find a link to prayer in tongues, and the scholar Gordon Fee has argued that tongues are probably in view. Most commentators (Cranfield, Moo, Dunn) say the groans are the Spirit's own prayer within believers, never uttered aloud. The Orthodox tradition of wordless prayer and the Catholic Catechism (741) both take the verse as the Spirit praying in us. The surrounding verses (8:23, 26) put the groaning of creation, of believers and of the Spirit in one chain.

p: The Old Testament's title for God as the one who knows what is inside.
b: God "searches" the heart in Psalm 139:1-2, Jeremiah 17:10 and Revelation 2:23; in 1 Samuel 16:7 and 1 Kings 8:39 the Hebrew says the Lord "looks at" or "knows" the heart, the same idea in other words. Paul gives it a new use: the One who searches hearts knows what the Spirit means, even when we cannot say it. The statement "in line with God" (kata theon) is literally "according to God," and many versions supply "the will of": the Spirit prays as God would have it. "The saints," here, are all believers (see 1:7, an earlier part). The verse is a comfort for those who do not know what to pray, which is the point of 8:26.

a: all things work together toward good
p: A famous promise. Paul's 'good' is the goal of 8:29, not comfort for every moment.
b: The verse is often taken to mean that every event, however bad, turns out well for believers. The Greek says something narrower: for those who love God, all things work together for their "good," and verse 29 defines that good as being shaped into the image of Christ. Commentators (Moo, Wright, Cranfield) stress that Paul does not call suffering good, but says God uses it for that goal. The text also has a variant: some early manuscripts (Papyrus 46, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus) have "God" as the subject, "God works all things together." "Those who love God" shows who is meant, and "called according to his purpose" says that the call comes from God's side. Compare Genesis 50:20, where Joseph tells his brothers that God turned their harm to good.
orig: πάντα συνεργεῖ εἰς ἀγαθόν (panta synergei eis agathon)

p: In the Bible 'know' often means 'choose in love'. The churches disagree about what Paul means.
b: Proginosko means "to know before." In the Hebrew Bible "to know" can mean choosing and caring for: God says of Israel that he alone has known them of all the families of the earth (Amos 3:2), and the Hebrew of Genesis 18:19 says "I have known him" of Abraham, where this site's Plain has "I have chosen him" (Genesis 18:19). Readings: (1) God's foreknowledge is a loving choice made beforehand (Augustine, the Reformed; Murray, Cranfield); (2) God foresees who will have faith, and chooses on that basis (Origen, Chrysostom, Arminius, Wesley, the Eastern tradition in general); (3) Molina's "middle knowledge" (what free creatures would do in any situation). Paul gives no reason for the choice here; the card below gives the traditions side by side.

p: The Greek verb is 'set the boundary beforehand'. It is the word behind 'predestine'.
b: Proorizo comes from horizo, "mark out a boundary" (our word "horizon"); it is used of what God had decided in Acts 4:28 and Ephesians 1:5, 11. The Plain says "decided beforehand" so the reader does not need the technical word "predestine." What is decided here is not who goes to heaven or hell, but a destination: being "formed to match the image of his Son." Barth read the passage as God's election of all people in Christ; the Reformed tradition reads it as election of particular people, and Arminians as election of those foreseen to believe. Wesley held that predestination in this verse means God's purpose for a type of people (those who believe).

a: formed to match the image of his Son
t: The image of the Son: Adam's calling restored
p: God made humans in his image (Genesis 1). The goal is to be like the Son, who is the true image.
b: "The image" (eikon) recalls Genesis 1:26-27: "Let us make humankind in our image, as our likeness." The Adam theme of chapters 5-8 comes back: humanity was to share God's image and was ruined; Christ, "the image of the invisible God" (Colossians 1:15), is the pattern of the restored human. The goal of 8:29, then, is not only being saved from punishment but being made like him. The Eastern church calls this theosis (becoming like God by sharing his life); the Western tradition speaks of conformity to Christ and sanctification; both read the verse along with 8:17 and 8:30 ("glorified"). Christ is the "firstborn" among many "brothers," a word that here means sisters too (Psalm 89:27 gives the title to the king; Colossians 1:15, 18 to Christ).

a: he glorified the ones he justified
p: All five verbs are in the past, as if the end were already done. The chain has no gap.
b: The five steps are foreknew, decided beforehand, called, justified, glorified (8:29-30), all in the past tense, though glorification is still future (8:17-18). Scholars take this as a "prophetic past": for God the end is certain, so Paul can speak as if complete. Puritan William Perkins called the series "the golden chain." Two points are noted. First, sanctification is not named (it is part of "formed to match"). Second, none of the verbs says "some of those called were not justified": the chain moves without a break. The Reformed read it as secure for the elect; Arminians read the chain as concerning those who stay in faith; the card below.

a: If God is for us, who is against us?
p: Psalm 118:6 and Isaiah 50:7-9 lie behind the questions of 8:31-34.
b: Psalm 118:6 begins "With the LORD for me, I have no fear." Isaiah 50:7-9 is a trial scene in which the Servant asks who will argue with him and who will condemn him, because the Lord God helps him. Paul's questions in 8:31-34 ("who is against us?" "who will accuse?" "who is there to condemn?") use these. The chapter began with "no condemnation" (8:1) and ends with the same ruling spoken as an argument: the court is closed. This is also the end of the argument of chapters 5-8: 8:31-39 sums up everything from 5:1.

a: He did not hold back his own Son.
p: The words come from the story of Abraham and Isaac. Some Jewish and Christian readers see a link on purpose.
b: God said to Abraham, "you have not held back your son, your only one" (Genesis 22:12). The promise is repeated at Genesis 22:16. The Greek Old Testament uses the same verb, "spare." Paul's "his own Son" (the adjective idios sharpens it) and "did not hold back" very likely echo that story, where Abraham is not asked to go through with it. Jewish tradition made the "binding of Isaac" (the Akedah) a source of merit and atonement; Jon Levenson's book discusses how Christians and Jews have read it. Here God does what Abraham was spared from doing. "Handed over" is the language of Isaiah 53:6, 12 in the Septuagint and the verb of Romans 4:25.

a: God is the one who justifies them
p: The Greek has no punctuation. Some editors read 'Is it God who justifies?'
b: The old manuscripts have no question marks, so 8:33-34 can be punctuated in more than one way. Statements: "God is the one who justifies. Who is there to condemn?" (this Plain, and most translations). Questions: "Is it God who justifies? Is it Christ who died?" which expects the answer "no, never": some readers have punctuated it so (Erasmus discusses the other reading). The sense most favored today is statements, which fits the flow of "no condemnation." "God's chosen" is Israel's title now given to all believers (Isaiah 43:20; 65:9). It is the first time "chosen" appears in Romans; chapter 9 takes up the theme.

t: Christ at God's right hand pleading
