p: Psalm 110:1 and the Servant of Isaiah 53 stand behind this. Hebrews and 1 John say the same.
b: "At God's right hand" is Psalm 110:1, the most-quoted Old Testament verse in the New Testament. "He pleads for us" says that Christ continues to act for believers: Hebrews 7:25 says he "always lives to plead for them," and 1 John 2:1 calls him an advocate with the Father. Isaiah 53:12 adds that the Servant "will step in for the rebels." The verb is the same as in 8:27, where the Spirit pleads. The Spirit pleads within us, the Son at God's right hand: the two intercessions meet the same need. Protestants have taught that this excludes any other mediator; Catholics and Orthodox answer that the saints' prayers join Christ's and do not replace it.

t: A list of ordeals, and 'the sword'
p: Paul lists what believers faced. 'The sword' ties to the state's power in 13:4.
b: The list (thlipsis, stenochoria, diogmos, limos, gymnotes, kindynos, machaira) belongs to a type that philosophers also wrote, the "catalogue of hardships," and Paul uses it for himself (1 Corinthians 4:9-13; 2 Corinthians 4:8-9; 6:4-10; 11:23-28). Rome in 57 had no empire-wide persecution; Nero's attack on the Christians came in 64 (Tacitus, Annals 15.44). But believers lived with poverty, hostility and the threat of arrest (see Acts 18:2 on the Jews expelled from Rome). "The sword" (machaira) is the same word used at 13:4 for the sword the governing authority "does not carry for nothing," so the two sides of Paul's teaching on the state meet here.

a: For your sake we are facing death all day long.
p: A psalm of innocent suffering. The Talmud applies the same verse to the martyrs.
b: Paul quotes Psalm 44:22 (43:23 in the Greek Bible) nearly word for word from the Septuagint. This site's Plain of the Hebrew says that "it is on your account that we are killed all day long" (Psalm 44:22). The psalm is a lament of a people who suffer although they have not forsaken God (Psalm 44:17-22): suffering is not explained as punishment. The Talmud tells of a mother with seven sons killed for refusing idolatry, who quotes this verse (Gittin 57b; compare 2 Maccabees 7). Paul uses it for the sufferings of 8:35, as the way of all God's people. For him it is not a sign of God's rejection but a reason for greater trust.

p: The Greek is a single compound verb: to be super-victorious. The empire's language was 'invincible'.
b: Hypernikao appears only here in the New Testament. It builds on nike, "victory," and means to win a victory that goes beyond. Roman imagery of victory (the goddess Victoria, the triumphal parade) was everywhere in the capital. Paul's victory is "through the One who loved us," and it comes in the very middle of "these things": hardship, not after it. He is not promising escape from the sword, but that it cannot separate. The KJV's "more than conquerors" is familiar. The Plain reads it as "win an overwhelming victory" to keep the single verb.

p: Angels, rulers and powers are most often read as heavenly beings. 'Height' and 'depth' may be star words.
b: "Angels, rulers (archai) and powers" are most often read as Paul's names for spiritual beings (Ephesians 1:21; Colossians 2:15; 1 Corinthians 15:24), which can be loyal or hostile; a few take "rulers" as human authorities. "Death nor life" and "things present nor things to come" cover the whole of time. "Height" (hypsoma) and "depth" (bathos) were used in ancient astrology for the highest and lowest points of a star's path; Paul may be saying that even the stars' rule over fate cannot separate. Others take them as simply all of space. The list ends with "any other created thing" (ktisis), the same word as "creation" in 8:19-22: nothing in creation, which suffers with us, has the power to separate.

t: The refrain that closes each section
p: Five sections of chapters 5-8 end the same way: through or in Jesus Christ our Lord.
b: Chapters 5-8 are marked off by a refrain: 5:21 ("through Jesus Christ our Lord"), 6:23 ("in Christ Jesus our Lord"), 7:25 ("through Jesus Christ our Lord"), 8:39 ("in Christ Jesus our Lord"), and earlier 5:11. Each tells the reader that a section is complete, which helps with the outline: justification and peace (5:1-11), Adam and Christ (5:12-21), sin (6:1-23), law (7:1-25), Spirit (8:1-39). The last verse is also the end of the whole third movement of the letter. The words "the love of God ... in Christ Jesus" answer the opening "peace with God" of 5:1, forming a ring around the section.
